books.section: Topic 1.6 Cultural Interactions Between Europeans, Native Americans, and Africans
Topic 1.5 Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

options.text: It made Spaniards the majority of the colonial population.
options.misconception: Spaniards stayed a tiny minority, one or two percent, even as mixed populations grew.

options.text: It created new social categories that had not existed before.
It stopped all further mixing between peoples.
options.misconception: Mixing continued and the categories kept multiplying; it never stopped.

options.text: It ended the system that ranked people by ancestry.
options.misconception: Mixing produced the categories of the casta system; it did not end ranking by ancestry.

rationales.general:
1. Ask what mestizos and mulattos were. People of mixed ancestry, new to the colonial world.
2. Ask what Spain did with them. It named them, counted them, and placed them in a ranked order.
3. Ask what that means. A new population created new social categories that had not existed before.
4. Rule out the rest. Ranking did not end, Spaniards did not become a majority, and mixing did not stop.
Remember: when a new group appears, ask what new labels the society invents for it.
rationales.B: Mestizos and mulattos were new kinds of people in the colonial world, and the Spanish named them, counted them, and ranked them. Mixing created social categories that had no place in Spain or in pre-contact America.
rationales.A: Spaniards remained one or two percent of the population. Growth in mixed populations did not make them a majority.
rationales.C: Mixing did not stop. The categories kept multiplying precisely because people kept mixing.
rationales.D: Ranking by ancestry did not end; it grew more detailed as mixing produced more categories to rank.

stem: Over time, intermarriage produced a large population of mestizos and mulattos. What did this growth change in Spanish America?

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, summarizing Barron's Premium 2027 Chapter 3, Topic 1.5 and Topic 1.6; Princeton Review Chapter 6.
stimulus.text: In Spain's American colonies, Spaniards were always greatly outnumbered by Native peoples, and Spanish men greatly outnumbered Spanish women. In these circumstances, intermarriage was common. The children of Spanish men and Indigenous women were called mestizos, and they made up four to five percent of the population. The children of Spanish men and African women were called mulattos. Over time, mixing produced a large population of people of mixed ancestry.
